question: Did Whitfield's conduct—concentrating elderly, moderate-risk-tolerance retirees into speculative micro-cap stocks, exercising unauthorized discretion, and mismarking solicited orders as unsolicited—violate Regulation BI, FINRA Rule 2111, and related FINRA rules?
answer:
Whitfield's conduct constitutes multiple overlapping violations of Regulation BI, FINRA Rule 2111, FINRA Rules 3260(b), 4511, and 2010.

First, for recommendations made on or after June 30, 2020, Whitfield willfully violated SEC Rule 15l-1(a)(1) (Regulation BI). The Care Obligation under Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(ii) requires that an associated person exercise reasonable diligence, care, and skill to have a reasonable basis to believe a recommendation is in the best interest of a particular retail customer, based on that customer's investment profile—including age, financial situation and needs, investment objectives, risk tolerance, time horizon, liquidity needs, and investment experience. Engstrom was a 74-year-old retiree with limited investment experience, a moderate risk tolerance, income-and-preservation objectives, and a 5-10 year horizon. Concentrating 84% of her liquid net worth in pre-revenue biotechnology and early-stage mining micro-caps is fundamentally incompatible with every material element of her investment profile. The same analysis applies to Johansson, whose 78% concentration in speculative equities contradicted his moderate risk tolerance and growth-and-income objective. No reasonable associated person exercising diligence, care, and skill could conclude these recommendations were in either customer's best interest.

For recommendations made prior to June 30, 2020, the identical fact pattern establishes a violation of FINRA Rule 2111's suitability requirement, which uses the same investment profile factors. The customer-specific suitability obligation under Rule 2111.05 required Whitfield to have a reasonable basis to believe the recommended securities were suitable for each particular customer. Both Engstrom's and Johansson's profiles made speculative concentration plainly unsuitable.

Second, Whitfield violated FINRA Rule 3260(b) by exercising discretion in 214 trades across 31 accounts without obtaining prior written authorization from customers or written acceptance of the accounts as discretionary by Meridian Securities. Rule 3260(b) explicitly prohibits a registered representative from exercising discretionary power in a customer's account unless the customer has given prior written authorization and the member firm has accepted the account as discretionary in writing.

Third, Whitfield violated FINRA Rule 4511 by mismarking 412 solicited trades as unsolicited across 38 accounts. Rule 4511 requires members and associated persons to make and preserve books and records as required under FINRA rules and applicable securities laws. Systematically mismarking order tickets as unsolicited falsifies the books and records of the firm and, critically, undermines the firm's ability to conduct supervisory review of the representative's recommendation activity.

All three categories of misconduct also independently violate FINRA Rule 2010's requirement to observe high standards of commercial honor and just and equitable principles of trade. The mismarking, in particular, was not merely a record-keeping lapse—it functioned as a deliberate mechanism to evade supervisory detection of the pattern of unsuitable and non-best-interest recommendations, compounding the severity of the violations.
applicable_standard: SEC Rule 15l-1(a)(1) (Regulation BI); SEC Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(ii) (Care Obligation); FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability); FINRA Rule 3260(b) (Discretionary Accounts); FINRA Rule 4511 (Books and Records); FINRA Rule 2010 (Standards of Commercial Honor)
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: Whitfield concentrated elderly, moderate-risk-tolerance retirees overwhelmingly into speculative micro-cap stocks in direct contradiction of their stated investment profiles, while exercising unauthorized discretion and mismarking solicited trades to evade supervisory detection.

fact_pattern:
Greenfield Wealth Advisors, LLC ('Greenfield') is a dual-registrant firm based in Denver, Colorado, registered as both an investment adviser under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 and a broker-dealer with FINRA. In March 2022, Greenfield's chief marketing officer, Dana Prescott, launched a new 'ESG Premier' advisory program marketed to retail investors as providing 'rigorously screened, best-in-class ESG portfolios aligned with your values.' The program was offered through both the advisory and brokerage channels, with the brokerage side recommending ESG-labeled mutual funds and ETFs on a transactional basis, and the advisory side managing discretionary ESG model portfolios for a 1.35% annual wrap fee.

One of Greenfield's registered representatives, Marcus Hale, recommended the ESG Premier brokerage product to 74-year-old retired schoolteacher Elaine Garza in April 2022. Mrs. Garza had a moderate risk tolerance, $430,000 in rollover IRA assets, a stated investment objective of capital preservation with modest income, and had expressed a general interest in 'doing something good with her money.' Hale recommended she invest $310,000 across three ESG-labeled mutual funds: the Verdant Global Impact Fund (Class A shares, 5.25% front-end load, 0.92% expense ratio), the CleanTech Growth Fund (Class C shares, 1.85% expense ratio with a 1% CDSC), and the Sustainable Income Bond Fund (Class A shares, 3.50% front-end load, 0.78% expense ratio). All three funds were on Greenfield's approved product list. Greenfield received revenue-sharing payments from two of the three fund families totaling approximately $14,500 annually based on assets placed.

Hale did not document any analysis comparing the recommended ESG funds to lower-cost ESG index ETFs available on the platform that tracked similar strategies with expense ratios between 0.10% and 0.25% and no sales loads. The Form CRS delivered to Mrs. Garza at account opening was a 2020 version that did not reflect Greenfield's updated revenue-sharing arrangements or the ESG Premier program. Greenfield's written supervisory procedures for Reg BI compliance had not been updated since their initial adoption in June 2020, and contained no specific protocols for evaluating ESG product claims against actual fund holdings, nor any procedures for documenting the cost-component analysis required under Reg BI's Care Obligation. During an SEC Division of Examinations sweep in September 2022, examiners flagged these deficiencies.
question: Did Marcus Hale's recommendation of the ESG-labeled mutual funds to Elaine Garza, and Greenfield's related supervisory framework, satisfy the requirements of Regulation Best Interest?
answer:
No. Hale's recommendation and Greenfield's supervisory infrastructure failed to satisfy multiple components of Regulation Best Interest (17 CFR §240.15l-1), and the deficiencies are compounding.

**Care Obligation (Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(ii)(B)):** Reg BI's Care Obligation requires that a broker-dealer exercise reasonable diligence, care, and skill in making a recommendation, including understanding the potential risks, rewards, and costs of the recommendation, and having a reasonable basis to believe the recommendation is in the retail customer's best interest at the time it is made. Here, Hale recommended Class A shares with a 5.25% front-end load and Class C shares with a 1.85% expense ratio to a 74-year-old retiree with a capital preservation objective. The platform offered substantially similar ESG index ETFs with expense ratios of 0.10%–0.25% and no loads. The cost differential on $310,000 is dramatic: the front-end loads alone consumed approximately $14,400 of Mrs. Garza's retirement capital. Hale documented no reasonably diligent analysis comparing these cost structures. Without such documentation — and absent any articulable rationale for why the higher-cost share classes served Mrs. Garza's specific needs better than available alternatives — the Care Obligation is not satisfied. The SEC has repeatedly emphasized in risk alerts (e.g., the April 2022 Staff Bulletin on Standards of Conduct) that cost is a critical factor, particularly for investors with income and preservation objectives.

**Disclosure Obligation (Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(ii)(A)):** Greenfield delivered an outdated 2020 Form CRS that omitted the revenue-sharing arrangements generating $14,500 annually and failed to disclose material conflicts associated with the ESG Premier program. Reg BI requires full and fair disclosure of all material facts relating to conflicts of interest associated with the recommendation. Revenue-sharing creates a direct financial incentive to recommend specific fund families, and its omission is a clear disclosure failure.

**Conflict of Interest Obligation (Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(ii)(C)):** Greenfield was required to establish, maintain, and enforce written policies and procedures reasonably designed to identify and mitigate conflicts of interest, including those arising from revenue-sharing. The firm's written supervisory procedures were stale — unchanged since June 2020 — and contained no protocols for the ESG Premier program, no cost-comparison methodology, and no framework to assess whether ESG marketing claims matched actual fund holdings. This represents a systemic compliance infrastructure failure.

**ESG-Specific Concerns:** Consistent with the 2022 Examination Priorities' focus on ESG investing (Section I.B), examiners scrutinize whether ESG claims are substantiated and whether firms have policies to evaluate ESG product labeling. Greenfield's lack of any procedure to verify ESG fund holdings against marketing claims heightens the risk of misleading recommendations.

Greenfield cannot credibly assert that Hale's recommendations were consistent with Reg BI. The combination of undocumented cost analysis, stale disclosures, undisclosed revenue-sharing conflicts, and absent ESG-specific supervisory procedures constitutes a multi-pronged violation.
applicable_standard: Regulation Best Interest (17 CFR §240.15l-1), including Care Obligation §240.15l-1(a)(2)(ii)(B), Disclosure Obligation §240.15l-1(a)(2)(ii)(A), Conflict of Interest Obligation §240.15l-1(a)(2)(ii)(C); Form CRS (17 CFR §240.17a-14); FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability); SEC 2022 Division of Examinations Priorities (ESG Investing, Standards of Conduct sections)
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: Hale failed to document any cost-comparison analysis between high-load ESG mutual funds and substantially similar low-cost ESG ETFs available on the same platform, defeating the Care Obligation's requirement of reasonable diligence in assessing costs relative to reasonably available alternatives.

fact_pattern:
Greenleaf Wealth Partners, LLC ('Greenleaf') is a dually registered investment adviser and broker-dealer based in Scottsdale, Arizona, with approximately $1.2 billion in assets under management. In January 2015, Greenleaf's management directed its 38 financial adviser representatives to begin migrating existing brokerage clients into fee-based advisory accounts charging a 1.25% annual asset-based fee. The initiative was internally referred to as 'Project Elevation.' Between January and September 2015, Greenleaf transitioned approximately 1,400 client accounts—representing roughly $340 million in assets—from commission-based brokerage accounts to fee-based advisory accounts.

Among the affected clients was Margaret Ellison, age 72, a retired schoolteacher in Mesa, Arizona, with a $485,000 portfolio consisting primarily of 15 individual investment-grade municipal bonds, three certificates of deposit, and a single S&P 500 index fund. Mrs. Ellison's account had generated only $380 in total commissions over the prior 24 months because her holdings were buy-and-hold, income-oriented positions that required minimal trading. Her financial adviser, Kevin Driscoll, moved her account into Greenleaf's 'Premier Advisory Program' in March 2015 without conducting any updated suitability analysis or investment profile review. Under the new fee-based arrangement, Mrs. Ellison was charged $6,062.50 in advisory fees during the first twelve months—a roughly 1,500% increase in total costs—despite no meaningful change in her investment strategy, no additional financial planning services, and no increase in the frequency of portfolio reviews. The Form ADV Part 2A brochure delivered to Mrs. Ellison at the time of the transition contained boilerplate language about fee-based accounts offering 'alignment of interests' and 'ongoing portfolio monitoring,' but did not disclose that her prior brokerage arrangement would likely have been significantly less expensive given her trading pattern.

Greenleaf's Chief Compliance Officer, Diana Reyes, had flagged the initiative in a February 2015 memo to management, noting that clients with low trading activity could be harmed by the transition and recommending individualized cost-benefit analyses before any migration. Management overruled the recommendation, citing competitive pressures and the desire for 'more predictable revenue streams.' No individualized analyses were performed for any of the 1,400 transitioned accounts. Internal emails later revealed that Greenleaf's representatives received a one-time $500 bonus per account transitioned, creating an additional financial incentive to move clients regardless of suitability.
question: Did Greenleaf Wealth Partners and its representative Kevin Driscoll violate their fiduciary and regulatory obligations by transitioning Margaret Ellison's low-activity brokerage account to a fee-based advisory account without conducting an individualized cost-benefit analysis?
answer:
Yes, Greenleaf and Driscoll violated multiple fiduciary and regulatory obligations. The conduct constitutes a textbook case of 'reverse churning'—the practice of placing a client in a fee-based advisory account where the ongoing asset-based fee substantially exceeds any benefit the client derives, particularly when the client's trading activity is minimal and the advisory services provided are negligible.

First, under Investment Advisers Act §206(1) and (2), investment advisers owe clients a fiduciary duty that encompasses both a duty of care and a duty of loyalty. The duty of care requires that an adviser provide advice that is in the client's best interest, including ensuring that the fee arrangement is suitable in light of the services actually rendered. By migrating Mrs. Ellison—a buy-and-hold retiree whose commission costs were $380 over two years—into an account costing over $6,000 annually with no incremental services, Greenleaf breached its duty of care. The duty of loyalty was also breached because the transition was motivated by Greenleaf's desire for predictable revenue and incentivized by the $500-per-account bonus paid to representatives, creating an undisclosed material conflict of interest.

Second, the 2015 OCIE examination priorities explicitly identified 'Fee Selection and Reverse Churning' as a focus area, noting that where an adviser offers a variety of fee arrangements, examiners will scrutinize 'recommendations of account types and whether they are in the best interest of the client at the inception of the arrangement and thereafter, including fees charged, services provided, and disclosures made.' Greenleaf's wholesale migration without individualized analysis directly implicates this priority.

Third, to the extent Driscoll acted in his broker-dealer capacity when recommending the transition, FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability) required a reasonable basis for believing the recommendation was suitable based on the customer's investment profile. No updated investment profile review was conducted, and the dramatically higher cost was unjustified by any change in strategy or services. The quantitative suitability component—while typically applied to excessive trading—is analogous here: the cost-to-benefit ratio was grossly disproportionate.

Fourth, the Form ADV Part 2A disclosure was inadequate under Advisers Act §204 and Rule 204-3 because it used boilerplate language about 'alignment of interests' without disclosing the material fact that Mrs. Ellison's prior arrangement was far less costly given her trading pattern. The CCO's documented warning, which management overruled, further demonstrates that Greenleaf had actual knowledge of the potential harm and consciously disregarded it. This aggravating factor would likely elevate any enforcement action beyond a simple compliance deficiency to potential fraud charges under §206.

Greenleaf cannot defend on grounds that the client received the ADV brochure, as boilerplate disclosure does not satisfy fiduciary obligations when the adviser knows the specific client will be disadvantaged.
applicable_standard: Investment Advisers Act §206(1)-(2) (anti-fraud/fiduciary duty); Investment Advisers Act §204 and Rule 204-3 (Form ADV delivery and disclosure); FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability); OCIE 2015 Examination Priorities (Fee Selection and Reverse Churning)
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: Greenleaf transitioned a low-activity, buy-and-hold retiree into a fee-based advisory account that increased her costs by approximately 1,500% without conducting any individualized cost-benefit analysis, while its CCO's written warning was overruled and representatives were paid per-account bonuses to incentivize the migration.

fact_pattern:
Apex Digital Advisors, LLC ('Apex'), a registered investment adviser that registered with the SEC in reliance on the Internet adviser exemption under Advisers Act Rule 203A-2(e), launched its robo-advisory platform 'SmartNest' in March 2019 to provide automated portfolio management to retail investors and participants in employer-sponsored 401(k) plans. By September 2021, SmartNest managed approximately $1.8 billion in assets across 42,000 individual accounts and 15 employer-sponsored retirement plans covering roughly 28,000 participants.

SmartNest's onboarding process required new clients to complete a 7-question online risk tolerance questionnaire. The questionnaire asked about the client's age, annual income, investment time horizon, and general comfort with market volatility, but did not inquire about the client's existing assets outside the platform, outstanding liabilities (such as mortgage debt or student loans), liquidity needs, tax situation, or specific financial goals beyond retirement. Based solely on the questionnaire responses, Apex's proprietary algorithm assigned each client to one of five model portfolios ranging from 'Conservative' (80% fixed income / 20% equities) to 'Aggressive Growth' (10% fixed income / 90% equities, including a 15% allocation to a proprietary ETF, Apex Growth Fund (ticker: APXG), managed by Apex's affiliated entity, Apex Fund Management, LLC). The algorithm's default setting automatically placed any client under age 35 into the Aggressive Growth portfolio unless the client manually selected a different risk level—a feature buried three screens deep in the settings menu.

Margaret Chen, a 29-year-old school teacher in Austin, Texas earning $52,000 annually, opened a SmartNest account in June 2020 and contributed $38,000 of her savings. Margaret had $87,000 in outstanding student loan debt and was saving for a home down payment she planned to make within two years. Because the questionnaire never asked about her liquidity needs, debt obligations, or near-term goals, the algorithm placed her entirely in the Aggressive Growth portfolio. During the market correction in September 2021, Margaret's portfolio lost approximately $7,600 (20%), severely impacting her ability to make her planned down payment. Apex's Form ADV Part 2A disclosed that 'portfolios are constructed using an algorithm that considers client-reported information' but did not disclose the age-based default assignment methodology or the conflict of interest arising from the 15% allocation to the affiliated APXG fund, which charged a 0.65% expense ratio—nearly double the 0.35% expense ratio of a comparable unaffiliated index ETF.

During a Division of Examinations sweep under the Electronic Investment Advice Initiative in October 2021, examiners found that Apex had not updated its risk questionnaire since the platform's 2019 launch, had no written policies or procedures governing periodic review or validation of the algorithm's suitability determinations, and had received 214 client complaints about inappropriate portfolio assignments over the prior 18 months without escalating the issue to the Chief Compliance Officer.
question: Did Apex Digital Advisors breach its fiduciary duty under the Investment Advisers Act by failing to adequately capture client investment profiles through its risk tolerance questionnaire, failing to disclose its age-based default assignment methodology and affiliated fund conflict, and failing to adopt and implement adequate compliance policies and procedures?
answer:
Apex Digital Advisors committed multiple violations of the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 and related obligations. The analysis proceeds on three grounds.

First, Apex breached its fiduciary duty of care under the Advisers Act by failing to act in its clients' best interests. Under SEC guidance, including the Division of Investment Management's February 2017 Guidance Update on Robo-Advisers, a robo-adviser must ensure that its client profiling process gathers sufficient information to form a reasonable basis for its investment recommendations. Apex's 7-question questionnaire omitted critical financial profile elements—outstanding liabilities, liquidity needs, near-term financial goals, outside assets, and tax considerations. As the eIA Risk Alert explicitly warns, when 'a robo-adviser's client survey process does not appropriately capture a client's risk tolerance, it could result in advice to invest in securities that are not aligned with the client's best interest.' Margaret Chen's situation is a textbook example: a 29-year-old with $87,000 in student debt and a two-year home purchase timeline was algorithmically placed into a 90% equity portfolio solely because of her age. This constitutes a failure of the duty of care.

Second, Apex breached its fiduciary duty of loyalty and violated Advisers Act Section 206(1) and 206(2) by failing to disclose material conflicts of interest. The 15% default allocation to the affiliated APXG fund—which carried expense ratios nearly double those of comparable alternatives—constituted a conflict that Apex was required to fully and fairly disclose. The Form ADV Part 2A's generic statement that 'portfolios are constructed using an algorithm that considers client-reported information' was insufficient to inform clients of either the age-based default override or the affiliated fund allocation. Under Section 206(2), an adviser engages in a fraudulent or deceptive act when it fails to disclose material conflicts, regardless of intent. Apex's omission satisfies this standard.

Third, Apex violated Advisers Act Section 206(4) and Rule 206(4)-7 (the Compliance Rule), which requires every registered adviser to adopt and implement written policies and procedures reasonably designed to prevent violations of the Advisers Act. Apex had no written procedures governing periodic review or validation of its algorithm's suitability determinations, had not updated the questionnaire in over two years despite evolving client demographics and market conditions, and failed to escalate 214 client complaints to the CCO. These facts demonstrate a systemic compliance failure, not an isolated oversight.

Apex cannot defend on the basis that clients voluntarily completed the questionnaire or that the settings menu theoretically allowed manual portfolio selection. A fiduciary cannot shift the burden to unsophisticated retail investors to discover and correct deficiencies in the adviser's own profiling methodology, particularly when the override mechanism was buried three screens deep. The totality of the facts—inadequate information gathering, undisclosed conflicts, affiliated fund self-dealing, and absent compliance infrastructure—constitutes a clear pattern of non-compliance identified as a core risk in the Division's eIA Initiative examinations.
applicable_standard: Investment Advisers Act of 1940 §§ 206(1), 206(2), 206(4); Advisers Act Rule 206(4)-7 (Compliance Rule); Advisers Act Rule 203A-2(e) (Internet Adviser Exemption); Advisers Act § 204 (Recordkeeping); SEC Division of Investment Management Guidance Update: Robo-Advisers (Feb. 23, 2017); SEC Division of Examinations eIA Risk Alert (Nov. 9, 2021)
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: Apex's risk tolerance questionnaire failed to capture critical client financial information—including liquidity needs, outstanding liabilities, and near-term goals—resulting in algorithmically generated portfolio assignments that were not aligned with clients' best interests, compounded by undisclosed conflicts from affiliated fund allocations.

fact_pattern:
Meridian Securities LLC is a dual-registered broker-dealer and investment adviser based in Arlington, Virginia, with approximately $2.3 billion in assets under advisement and 147 registered representatives. In March 2025, the SEC's Division of Examinations commenced a routine examination of Meridian focusing on Regulation Best Interest (Reg BI) compliance. During the exam, staff discovered that Meridian's Chief Operating Officer, Sandra Whitfield, had been responsible for a cost-reduction initiative launched in September 2024. As part of that initiative, Whitfield directed the firm's operations team to procure 85 refurbished laptop computers and 40 network switches from a third-party surplus dealer, Apex Resale Partners, for a total cost of $187,500. These devices were deployed across branch offices for use by registered representatives who accessed client portfolio management systems, custodial platforms, and the firm's order management system.

The examination staff found that the refurbished equipment had not been subjected to any supply chain risk assessment, and the laptops shipped with outdated operating systems (Windows 10, which had reached end-of-life support in October 2025). The network switches lacked current firmware and had no documented chain of custody from their original government or corporate owners. Meridian's written supervisory procedures (WSPs) referenced a cybersecurity policy requiring that all IT equipment meet NIST SP 800-53 controls, but Whitfield bypassed the internal IT security review process, justifying the decision as a 'cost-saving procurement measure.' No vulnerability scan, configuration audit, or secure wipe verification was performed before deployment.

During the same exam period, staff also reviewed a sample of 200 retail customer accounts and identified that 34 customers—primarily retirees aged 65-78 with moderate risk profiles and account sizes ranging from $120,000 to $475,000—had been recommended Class C shares of the Prestige Growth & Income Fund, which carried a 1.00% annual 12b-1 fee and a 1.00% contingent deferred sales charge (CDSC). An institutional share class of the same fund was available on Meridian's platform at a net expense ratio of 0.45% with no sales load, and these customers' account sizes qualified for the lower-cost share class. Meridian's compliance department had not updated its share class conflict disclosure since 2021, and the firm's Reg BI disclosure (Form CRS) did not mention the availability of lower-cost share classes for the specific fund family. Registered representative Derek Hollis, who handled 28 of the 34 accounts, received a 0.25% trailing commission on Class C shares that he would not have received on the institutional class.
question: Did Meridian Securities LLC violate Regulation Best Interest and its related component obligations by (a) recommending higher-cost share classes to retail customers without adequate disclosure or consideration of reasonably available alternatives, and (b) deploying unsecured IT equipment that could compromise client data, and what are the specific regulatory implications?
answer:
Meridian Securities LLC committed multiple violations implicating Regulation Best Interest (17 CFR §240.15l-1) and related supervisory obligations under FINRA Rules.

First, regarding the share class recommendations: Reg BI's Care Obligation (Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(ii)(B)) requires that a broker-dealer exercise reasonable diligence, care, and skill to understand the potential risks, rewards, and costs associated with a recommendation and have a reasonable basis to believe the recommendation is in the retail customer's best interest at the time it is made, considering reasonably available alternatives. Here, 34 retail customers—predominantly senior investors with moderate risk profiles—were placed in Class C shares carrying a combined cost burden of approximately 2.00% (1.00% 12b-1 plus potential CDSC), when a qualifying institutional share class at 0.45% was available on the firm's own platform. The $120,000-$475,000 account sizes clearly met institutional class thresholds. This represents a failure of the Care Obligation because Derek Hollis and Meridian failed to consider the reasonably available lower-cost alternative.

Additionally, the Conflict of Interest Obligation (Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(ii)(D)) required Meridian to establish, maintain, and enforce written policies and procedures reasonably designed to identify, disclose, and mitigate or eliminate material conflicts of interest. Hollis's 0.25% trailing commission on Class C shares created a direct financial incentive to recommend the higher-cost class. The firm's failure to update its conflict disclosures since 2021 and the omission of share class availability from Form CRS violated the Disclosure Obligation (Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(ii)(A)). This mirrors findings from the SEC's November 2020 Risk Alert on Reg BI examinations and the longstanding share-class selection disclosure initiative.

Second, the IT procurement issue implicates FINRA Rule 3110 (Supervision) and Regulation S-P (17 CFR §248.30), which requires broker-dealers to adopt written policies and procedures reasonably designed to safeguard customer records and information. Deploying 85 unvetted laptops with end-of-life operating systems and 40 network switches without firmware updates, chain-of-custody verification, or vulnerability scanning—while bypassing the firm's own NIST-aligned cybersecurity policies—creates material risk of unauthorized access to client data. The SEC's guidance on excess personal property procurement (OCOO.01, February 2025) illustrates that even the SEC itself requires rigorous supply chain and configuration review before deploying surplus IT equipment. A regulated entity holding sensitive retail customer data bears at least an equivalent duty.

Meridian cannot raise a cost-efficiency defense; Reg BI and supervisory obligations are not subject to budgetary convenience exceptions. The firm's WSPs were adequate on paper but were willfully circumvented, establishing a supervisory failure. The verdict is non-compliant on both counts, exposing Meridian to potential enforcement action, disgorgement of excess compensation, and remedial undertakings.
applicable_standard: Regulation Best Interest (17 CFR §240.15l-1), including Care Obligation (Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(ii)(B)), Disclosure Obligation (Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(ii)(A)), Conflict of Interest Obligation (Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(ii)(D)); FINRA Rule 3110 (Supervision); FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability); Regulation S-P (17 CFR §248.30); SEC Form CRS (17 CFR §249.640)
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: Meridian's registered representative received a 0.25% trailing commission on Class C shares while an available lower-cost institutional share class was never considered or disclosed, directly failing Reg BI's Care and Conflict of Interest Obligations.

fact_pattern:
NovaTech Digital Advisors, LLC ('NovaTech') is an SEC-registered investment adviser that launched its robo-advisory platform in January 2019, registering under the Internet adviser exemption pursuant to Advisers Act Rule 203A-2(e). By March 2023, NovaTech managed approximately $1.8 billion in assets across 47,000 individual retail accounts and approximately 120 employer-sponsored 401(k) plans covering 15,000 participants. NovaTech's platform uses a proprietary algorithm to construct and manage diversified ETF portfolios across five risk tiers: Conservative, Moderately Conservative, Balanced, Growth, and Aggressive Growth.

NovaTech's onboarding process includes a seven-question digital risk tolerance questionnaire ('RTQ'). The RTQ asks clients about their investment time horizon, annual income, net worth, and general comfort with market volatility, but does not ask about liquidity needs, existing debt obligations, concentration in employer stock (relevant for 401(k) participants), or near-term financial goals such as home purchases or college tuition. Additionally, the RTQ uses a static scoring methodology that has not been updated or back-tested since the platform's initial launch in 2019, despite significant changes in market conditions—including the COVID-19 sell-off and the 2022 rate-driven equity/bond drawdowns. NovaTech's compliance team flagged the RTQ's limitations in an internal memorandum dated September 2021, recommending the addition of at least four supplemental questions addressing liquidity and near-term cash needs. Senior management deferred the update to a future product release that, as of August 2023, had not been implemented.

In one illustrative case, Margaret Ellison, age 62, a participant in the Harbor Industries 401(k) plan serviced by NovaTech, completed the RTQ in April 2022. She indicated a five-year time horizon (reflecting her expected retirement at 67), household income of $95,000, and moderate comfort with volatility. Based solely on these inputs, the algorithm placed her in the 'Growth' tier—an 80% equity / 20% fixed income allocation—without ascertaining that she had $42,000 in outstanding consumer debt and planned to draw $60,000 from her 401(k) within 18 months to pay off that debt and fund a kitchen renovation. Ms. Ellison's Growth portfolio lost approximately 17.4% ($31,320 on a $180,000 balance) during the 2022 market downturn. Had the questionnaire captured her near-term liquidity need and debt profile, the algorithm would have placed her in the 'Moderately Conservative' tier (35% equity / 65% fixed income), which lost only 5.2% over the same period. NovaTech's Form ADV Part 2A brochure stated that the firm 'constructs portfolios tailored to each client's unique financial circumstances and risk profile,' without disclosing that the RTQ did not capture liquidity needs or near-term spending goals.
question: Did NovaTech Digital Advisors violate its fiduciary obligations under the Investment Advisers Act by failing to update its risk tolerance questionnaire and by omitting material questions regarding liquidity needs and near-term financial goals, resulting in unsuitable portfolio allocations for clients like Margaret Ellison?
answer:
Yes. NovaTech violated its fiduciary duty under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940, specifically the duty of care and duty of loyalty owed to advisory clients, as articulated in SEC v. Capital Gains Research Bureau, Inc., 375 U.S. 180 (1963), and as reinforced by the SEC's June 2019 Commission Interpretation Regarding Standard of Conduct for Investment Advisers (IA-5248). The Division of Examinations' 2021 Risk Alert on Electronic Investment Advice specifically identified deficient client survey processes—those that fail to appropriately capture a client's risk tolerance—as a key compliance concern that can result in advice misaligned with a client's best interest.

First, NovaTech's duty of care requires it to have a reasonable basis for the investment advice it provides, which necessarily includes a reasonable process for gathering client information. The RTQ's omission of questions regarding liquidity needs, outstanding debt, and near-term financial goals renders it materially deficient. Under Advisers Act §206(1) and §206(2), an adviser engages in fraud or deceit when it fails to obtain sufficient information to form a reasonable basis for its recommendations. The seven-question RTQ, which ignored liquidity and near-term cash demands, cannot support a 'reasonable belief' that the resulting allocation serves the client's best interest. The 2021 Risk Alert explicitly warns that if a robo-adviser's questionnaire 'does not appropriately capture a client's risk tolerance, it could result in advice to invest in securities that are not aligned with the client's best interest.'

Second, NovaTech's Form ADV Part 2A disclosure was materially misleading in violation of Advisers Act §206(4) and Rule 206(4)-1. The brochure represented that portfolios were 'tailored to each client's unique financial circumstances,' when in fact the RTQ systematically excluded key financial circumstances. This creates an inadequate and misleading disclosure, another specific deficiency category identified in the Risk Alert.

Third, NovaTech's internal compliance memorandum from September 2021 documenting the RTQ's deficiencies—and management's failure to act on it for nearly two years—undermines any defense of good faith and demonstrates a potential violation of Advisers Act §206(4) and Rule 206(4)-7 (compliance program requirements). An adviser's compliance policies must be reasonably designed to prevent violations; knowingly deferring a remediation of an identified deficiency is itself a compliance program failure.

Ms. Ellison's case concretely illustrates the harm: a $31,320 loss versus an estimated $9,360 loss had the questionnaire been adequate. NovaTech cannot defend by arguing automation alone satisfies its obligations; the fiduciary duty applies with equal force regardless of the delivery mechanism. The firm should have updated the RTQ, disclosed its limitations, or implemented a process for human review of edge cases involving retirement-age participants with near-term liquidity needs.
applicable_standard: Investment Advisers Act of 1940 §206(1), §206(2), §206(4); Rule 206(4)-1 (disclosure); Rule 206(4)-7 (compliance programs); Rule 203A-2(e) (Internet adviser exemption); SEC Interpretation Regarding Standard of Conduct for Investment Advisers (IA-5248, June 2019); OCIE/Division of Examinations Risk Alert: Observations from Examinations of Advisers that Provide Electronic Investment Advice (Nov. 9, 2021)
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: NovaTech's risk tolerance questionnaire systematically omitted questions regarding liquidity needs, near-term financial goals, and outstanding debt, resulting in unsuitable portfolio allocations that the firm's own compliance team had flagged but management failed to remediate for nearly two years.

fact_pattern:
Ridgewood Capital Advisors, LLC ('Ridgewood') is an SEC-registered investment adviser based in Hartford, Connecticut, with approximately $2.8 billion in assets under management. Ridgewood serves as the investment consultant to the Connecticut Municipal Employees' Pension Fund ('the Fund'), a defined benefit plan with $1.4 billion in total assets covering 12,000 active and retired municipal workers. In March 2022, Ridgewood's Chief Investment Officer, David Thornton, recommended that the Fund allocate $70 million — roughly 5% of total plan assets — to Pinnacle Offshore Partners, LP, a Cayman Islands-domiciled hedge fund employing a long/short credit strategy managed by Pinnacle Asset Management Group ('Pinnacle'). Thornton had attended a capital introduction dinner hosted by Pinnacle's prime broker, Goldman Sachs, in January 2022 and was impressed by the fund's purported 18.2% annualized net return over five years.

Ridgewood's written due diligence policy, last updated in 2019, required that before recommending any alternative investment to pension plan clients, the firm must: (1) conduct an onsite visit to the manager's offices; (2) independently verify assets under management through the fund administrator; (3) obtain and review position-level transparency or a transparency report from an independent risk aggregator; (4) perform comprehensive background checks on key personnel through a third-party provider; and (5) confirm the existence and independence of critical service providers including the auditor, administrator, and prime broker. Ridgewood's compliance manual further stated that these steps must be documented in an investment memorandum prior to any allocation.

In practice, Thornton bypassed several of these steps. No onsite visit was conducted; Thornton instead relied on a 45-minute Zoom call with Pinnacle's head of investor relations. Ridgewood did not independently verify Pinnacle's $900 million in reported AUM through the fund's administrator, Apex Fund Services, and instead accepted Pinnacle's self-reported figure from its marketing deck. No background checks were run on Pinnacle's portfolio manager, Marcus Webb, who — had a check been performed — would have revealed a 2017 FINRA bar for unauthorized trading at a prior broker-dealer. Ridgewood did not request or obtain any position-level transparency or independent transparency report. The only due diligence document produced was a two-page summary memo drafted by a junior analyst who had joined the firm three weeks earlier. The $70 million allocation was executed on April 15, 2022. By November 2022, Pinnacle had suspended redemptions, and the Fund ultimately recovered only $11.2 million of its investment after Pinnacle's collapse amid revelations of inflated NAV reporting.

During an SEC examination in Q1 2023, OCIE staff reviewed Ridgewood's due diligence files and identified the gaps between Ridgewood's written policies and its actual practices regarding the Pinnacle allocation.
question: Did Ridgewood Capital Advisors breach its fiduciary duty under the Investment Advisers Act and its own compliance policies in connection with the due diligence performed on the Pinnacle Offshore Partners allocation for the Connecticut Municipal Employees' Pension Fund?
answer:
Ridgewood Capital Advisors clearly breached its fiduciary duty under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940, and its conduct would likely be cited as deficient under Section 206(1) and (2) of the Advisers Act, which prohibit fraudulent, deceptive, or manipulative practices, as well as Section 206(4) and Rule 206(4)-7, which require advisers to adopt and implement written compliance policies and procedures reasonably designed to prevent violations. The Supreme Court's foundational holding in SEC v. Capital Gains Research Bureau, Inc., 375 U.S. 180 (1963), establishes that an investment adviser owes a fiduciary duty to act in its clients' best interests, encompassing a duty of care that necessarily includes the obligation to conduct reasonable investigation before making investment recommendations.

The OCIE Risk Alert at issue specifically identifies best practices for due diligence of alternative investments, including: (i) conducting onsite reviews; (ii) independently verifying assets through fund administrators; (iii) obtaining position-level transparency or independent transparency reports; (iv) having independent providers perform comprehensive background checks; and (v) confirming the independence and existence of critical service providers. Ridgewood's own written compliance policies incorporated each of these steps, yet the firm failed to execute any of them with respect to the Pinnacle allocation.

The failure is compounded by several factors. First, Ridgewood owed heightened duties as a pension consultant under ERISA §404(a)(1)(B), which requires fiduciaries to act with the 'care, skill, prudence, and diligence' of a prudent expert — the so-called 'prudent expert' standard. Allocating $70 million of pension assets based on a marketing deck and a brief video call with investor relations, without any independent verification, falls well below this standard. Second, the failure to conduct background checks on Marcus Webb, which would have revealed his FINRA bar under FINRA Rule 2111 considerations and general prudence requirements, represents a material gap — the very type of operational due diligence failure the Risk Alert warns against. Third, Ridgewood's reliance on a two-page memo drafted by a newly hired junior analyst demonstrates a failure to utilize experienced investment teams when evaluating complex strategies, another deficiency highlighted by OCIE.

Ridgewood cannot defend its conduct by arguing reliance on Pinnacle's representations; the fiduciary duty demands independent verification, not passive acceptance. The firm's written policies existed precisely because the complexity and opacity of alternative investments demand heightened scrutiny. The disconnect between Ridgewood's written procedures and its actual conduct constitutes a violation of Rule 206(4)-7's implementation requirement. The SEC has consistently held that adopting policies on paper without following them is itself a compliance failure. Ridgewood's conduct was non-compliant across multiple dimensions.
applicable_standard: Investment Advisers Act of 1940 §206(1), (2), and (4); Rule 206(4)-7 (Compliance Policies and Procedures); SEC v. Capital Gains Research Bureau, Inc., 375 U.S. 180 (1963); ERISA §404(a)(1)(B) (Prudent Expert Standard); OCIE Risk Alert on Investment Adviser Due Diligence Processes for Selecting Alternative Investments (Jan. 28, 2014)
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: Ridgewood systematically failed to follow its own written due diligence policies — including onsite visits, independent AUM verification, background checks, and position-level transparency review — before allocating $70 million of pension assets to an alternative investment manager whose principal had a prior FINRA bar.

fact_pattern:
Marcus Whitfield is a registered representative with Pinnacle Financial Services, a dually registered broker-dealer and investment adviser. In March 2024, Marcus contacts Helen Ostrowski, a 62-year-old public school teacher nearing retirement, after obtaining her information from a lead-generation service that targets participants in the state teachers' 403(b) plan. Helen has $387,000 in her 403(b) account, invested in a diversified portfolio of low-cost target-date funds with an all-in expense ratio of 0.12%. Marcus invites Helen to a complimentary 'retirement readiness workshop' at a local hotel, where he delivers a presentation emphasizing the risks of market volatility and the importance of guaranteed lifetime income in retirement.

Following the workshop, Marcus schedules an individual meeting with Helen. During this meeting, he recommends that she roll over her entire 403(b) balance into an individual retirement account (IRA) at Pinnacle, and then invest the proceeds in the Apex Secure Horizon Plus fixed indexed annuity, which carries a 10-year surrender charge schedule starting at 9%, an annual rider fee of 1.35% for a guaranteed lifetime withdrawal benefit, and a 1.15% annual spread charge. Marcus would receive a 6.5% upfront commission ($25,155) on the sale, plus a 0.25% trail commission. Marcus does not document any analysis comparing Helen's existing 403(b) plan investment options, fees, and available annuity options within the plan to the recommended IRA rollover and annuity purchase. He does not evaluate whether Helen's existing plan offers an institutional-share annuity with lower fees. His written recommendation to Helen states only that 'guaranteed income provides peace of mind in retirement' and that 'an IRA gives you more control over your money.'

Pinnacle's compliance department has a rollover review policy, but it requires only that the representative complete a one-page checklist confirming the client was informed of rollover options. The checklist does not require a quantitative comparison of plan fees, investment options, or a cost-benefit analysis of remaining in the existing plan versus rolling over. Marcus completes the checklist, checks all boxes, and the transaction is approved the same day. Helen signs the rollover paperwork and annuity application without receiving any written disclosure of the conflicts of interest arising from Marcus's compensation differential.
question: Under the DOL's proposed Retirement Security Rule and the existing/proposed requirements of PTE 2020-02, did Marcus and Pinnacle Financial Services satisfy their fiduciary obligations in connection with Helen's rollover recommendation and annuity purchase?
answer:
No. Marcus and Pinnacle Financial Services failed to satisfy their fiduciary obligations under both the proposed Retirement Security Rule's expanded definition of investment advice fiduciary and the conditions of PTE 2020-02, as proposed to be amended.

First, under the proposed Retirement Security Rule (RIN 1210-AC02), Marcus's recommendation that Helen roll over her 403(b) into an IRA would constitute fiduciary investment advice. The proposal broadens the definition under ERISA §3(21)(A)(ii) and IRC §4975(e)(3)(B) to capture one-time rollover recommendations made by persons who hold themselves out as providing individualized retirement advice for a fee or other compensation, which Marcus clearly does through the workshop and individual consultation.

As a fiduciary, Marcus's rollover recommendation triggers the prohibited transaction rules under ERISA §406(b) and IRC §4975(c)(1)(D)-(F), because the recommendation generates substantial variable compensation (6.5% upfront commission plus trails) that creates a direct conflict of interest. To rely on PTE 2020-02 for relief, both Marcus and Pinnacle must satisfy several conditions they plainly failed to meet.

Under PTE 2020-02 §II(a), the investment professional must provide advice in the "best interest" of the retirement investor, meaning the fiduciary must act with the care, skill, prudence, and diligence that a prudent person would exercise based on the investment objectives, risk tolerance, financial circumstances, and needs of the investor, without regard to the financial interests of the adviser. Marcus conducted no documented comparison of Helen's existing 403(b) plan costs (0.12% all-in) versus the recommended annuity (combined annual costs exceeding 2.50% plus a 9% surrender penalty). This omission is fatal.

Under PTE 2020-02 §II(b), specifically addressing rollover recommendations, the fiduciary must consider the existing plan's fees, available investment options, services, and potential penalty-free distribution features. Marcus performed none of this analysis. The one-page checklist used by Pinnacle does not constitute the specific rollover documentation the DOL requires under the exemption's conditions.

Under PTE 2020-02 §II(c) and (d), the financial institution must adopt and enforce written policies and procedures reasonably designed to ensure compliance with the Impartial Conduct Standards and must disclose material conflicts of interest, including compensation differentials. Pinnacle's perfunctory checklist policy falls far short of this requirement, and Marcus provided Helen no written conflict-of-interest disclosure.

The proposed amendments to PTE 2020-02 further tighten these requirements, making Pinnacle's same-day approval process and lack of quantitative analysis even more clearly deficient. Without satisfying PTE 2020-02's conditions, the transaction constitutes a non-exempt prohibited transaction under ERISA §406(b) and IRC §4975(c).
applicable_standard: ERISA §3(21)(A)(ii); ERISA §§404(a), 406(a), 406(b); IRC §4975(c)(1)(D)-(F); IRC §4975(e)(3)(B); PTE 2020-02 §§II(a)-(d); Proposed Retirement Security Rule (RIN 1210-AC02); Proposed Amendment to PTE 2020-02 (Application No. D-12057, RIN 1210-ZA32); 29 CFR 2550
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: Marcus failed to perform or document any comparative analysis of Helen's existing low-cost 403(b) plan options versus the higher-cost IRA annuity, as required by PTE 2020-02's rollover-specific conditions, rendering the prohibited transaction exemption unavailable.

fact_pattern:
Marcus Harding is a registered representative and investment adviser representative affiliated with Pinnacle Financial Partners, Inc., an independent broker-dealer and corporate RIA based in Des Moines, Iowa, with approximately 800 financial professionals. On March 12, 2024, Marcus met with Linda Kowalski, a 58-year-old public school teacher in Cedar Rapids, Iowa, who was considering what to do with her 403(b) plan after learning she would be eligible for early retirement in September 2024. Linda's 403(b) held $287,000, invested in a lineup of low-cost TIAA-CREF index funds with a blended expense ratio of 0.08%. Linda also had a small traditional IRA with $34,000 at a local bank, invested in a 12-month CD earning 4.85% APY.

During their meeting, Marcus recommended that Linda roll her 403(b) into a new IRA at Pinnacle, where he would manage the assets in a fee-based advisory account charging 1.25% annually. He also recommended consolidating the bank IRA into the same account for simplicity. Marcus prepared a financial plan projecting 7% annual growth and emphasized the benefits of 'holistic management' and 'personalized attention.' He did not document any comparison of the 403(b) plan's investment options, fees, or available services against the proposed IRA. He did not evaluate whether Linda could remain in the 403(b) post-separation or whether the plan offered any institutional share classes, stable value funds, or annuity guarantees that would be unavailable in a retail IRA.

Marcus's compensation would increase significantly from the rollover: he would earn approximately $3,587.50 annually in advisory fees on the combined $321,000, whereas he earned nothing from Linda's existing 403(b) or CD-based IRA. Pinnacle Financial Partners had a general rollover recommendation policy template but did not require advisers to complete a specific rollover comparison worksheet or document the basis for recommending a rollover over staying in the employer plan. Marcus submitted the rollover paperwork on April 3, 2024, and Linda's assets were transferred by April 22, 2024.
question: Under the DOL's proposed expanded fiduciary definition and the requirements of PTE 2020-02 as proposed to be amended, did Marcus Harding and Pinnacle Financial Partners satisfy their fiduciary obligations in connection with the rollover recommendation to Linda Kowalski?
answer:
No. Marcus Harding and Pinnacle Financial Partners failed to satisfy their fiduciary obligations under both the DOL's proposed expanded definition of investment advice fiduciary and the conditions of PTE 2020-02 as proposed to be amended.

First, under the proposed rule expanding the definition of 'investment advice for a fee' under ERISA §3(21)(A)(ii) and Internal Revenue Code §4975(e)(3)(B), Marcus's rollover recommendation to Linda clearly constitutes fiduciary investment advice. The proposed rule eliminates the prior five-part test and instead captures one-time recommendations — including rollover recommendations — made by persons who hold themselves out as providing individualized advice in exchange for a fee. Marcus met with Linda individually, presented a personalized financial plan, and would receive ongoing advisory fees from the rolled-over assets. This squarely falls within the proposed rule's broader fiduciary definition.

Second, because Marcus is a fiduciary receiving compensation that creates a conflict of interest (he earns 1.25% on rolled-over assets versus nothing on the 403(b)), the transaction is a prohibited transaction under ERISA §406(b) and IRC §4975(c)(1)(D)-(F). To rely on PTE 2020-02 for relief, Marcus and Pinnacle must satisfy several conditions, including the Impartial Conduct Standards requiring that the advice be in the customer's best interest at the time of the recommendation, that compensation be reasonable, and that no materially misleading statements be made. Critically, PTE 2020-02 as proposed to be amended specifically requires documentation of the specific reasons why a rollover recommendation is in the retirement investor's best interest, including a comparison of investment options, fees, and services available in the existing plan versus the recommended IRA.

Marcus performed no such comparison. He did not evaluate whether Linda could remain in the 403(b) post-retirement, did not compare the 0.08% blended expense ratio against the proposed 1.25% advisory fee, and did not assess whether TIAA-CREF's institutional products — including potential stable value or guaranteed income options — would be lost. The annual fee differential alone (approximately $3,350 more per year in the IRA) with no documented offsetting benefit strongly suggests the recommendation was not in Linda's best interest.

Pinnacle's supervisory failure compounds the violation. Under PTE 2020-02's amended provisions, the financial institution must establish, maintain, and enforce written policies and procedures to ensure compliance, including specific protocols for rollover recommendations. Pinnacle's generic template without a mandatory rollover comparison worksheet is insufficient. The pivotal failures are the absence of any documented comparative analysis and the significant fee disparity that was neither disclosed nor justified.
applicable_standard: ERISA §3(21)(A)(ii); ERISA §§404(a), 406(b); IRC §4975(c)(1)(D)-(F), §4975(e)(3)(B); PTE 2020-02 §II(a) Impartial Conduct Standards; PTE 2020-02 proposed amendments regarding rollover documentation requirements; DOL Proposed Rule 88 FR 75890 (Nov. 3, 2023); 29 CFR §2550.408b-2
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: Marcus failed to perform or document any comparison of the 403(b) plan's 0.08% expense ratio, institutional investment options, and post-separation availability against the proposed 1.25% fee-based IRA, rendering the rollover recommendation unsupported as being in Linda's best interest under PTE 2020-02.

fact_pattern:
Marcus Webley is a registered representative at Granite Peak Financial Services, a broker-dealer that also offers proprietary variable annuity products underwritten by its insurance affiliate, Granite Peak Life Insurance Company. On March 14, 2024, Marcus meets with Patricia Sandoval, a 58-year-old public school teacher who is retiring at the end of the school year. Patricia has accumulated $412,000 in her employer-sponsored 403(b) plan, which is invested in a diversified portfolio of low-cost Vanguard target-date funds with an all-in expense ratio of 0.12%. Patricia tells Marcus she is nervous about managing her money in retirement and wants 'someone to watch over it.' She says she has no other significant assets aside from her anticipated state pension of $3,200 per month.

Marcus recommends that Patricia roll over her entire $412,000 403(b) balance into a traditional IRA at Granite Peak, and invest the full amount into the Granite Peak Strategic Growth Variable Annuity, which carries a 1.35% mortality and expense risk charge, a 0.85% administrative fee, a 7-year declining surrender charge schedule starting at 7%, and underlying sub-account fees averaging 0.92%. The total annual cost of the annuity is approximately 3.12%. Marcus receives a 5.5% upfront commission of $22,660 on the sale, plus a 0.25% annual trail commission. The Granite Peak internal product bulletin, obtained during a subsequent compliance review, shows that Marcus was enrolled in a quarterly sales contest where the top seller of the Strategic Growth VA would receive a $10,000 bonus and an all-expenses-paid trip to Cabo San Lucas.

Marcus's rollover recommendation documentation consists of a one-page form that checks a box stating 'client desires professional management' and 'client wants guaranteed income options,' but does not include any comparative analysis of the fees in Patricia's existing 403(b) plan versus the proposed IRA annuity. Marcus does not disclose the sales contest to Patricia. His firm's compliance department had circulated a memo in January 2024 referencing the DOL's proposed Retirement Security Rule and reminding advisers to document rollover recommendations with detailed cost comparisons, but Marcus did not follow this guidance.
question: Under the DOL's proposed Retirement Security Rule and the conditions of PTE 2020-02, did Marcus Webley and Granite Peak Financial Services satisfy their fiduciary obligations in connection with the rollover recommendation and variable annuity sale to Patricia Sandoval?
answer:
No. Marcus Webley and Granite Peak Financial Services violated their fiduciary obligations under the DOL's proposed Retirement Security Rule and failed to satisfy the conditions necessary to rely on PTE 2020-02 for the conflicted transaction.

First, under the proposed Retirement Security Rule, Marcus's recommendation to roll over Patricia's 403(b) into an IRA constitutes fiduciary investment advice. The proposed rule broadens the definition of an investment advice fiduciary to encompass one-time recommendations—such as rollover recommendations—made by persons who hold themselves out as trusted advisers providing individualized recommendations. Marcus clearly held himself out as a knowledgeable professional making a personalized recommendation to Patricia, bringing him squarely within the proposed fiduciary definition. As a fiduciary, Marcus owes duties of prudence under ERISA §404(a)(1)(B) and loyalty under ERISA §404(a)(1)(A).

Second, the recommendation to invest the entirety of Patricia's $412,000 retirement savings into a proprietary variable annuity generating a 5.5% upfront commission and ongoing trail fees constitutes a prohibited transaction under ERISA §406(b), as Marcus received compensation that creates a direct conflict between his financial interest and Patricia's. To engage in this transaction lawfully, Marcus and Granite Peak must satisfy all conditions of PTE 2020-02.

PTE 2020-02 requires, among other things, that the fiduciary provide advice in the retirement investor's best interest, meaning the advice reflects the care, skill, prudence, and diligence that a prudent person would exercise based on the investment objectives, risk tolerance, financial circumstances, and needs of the investor, without placing the financial interest of the adviser ahead of the investor's interest. The exemption further requires that financial institutions establish policies and procedures designed to mitigate conflicts of interest and that compensation not be based on sales contests or quotas with respect to specific products.

Marcus failed these conditions on multiple grounds. The 3.12% total annual cost of the variable annuity versus the 0.12% cost of Patricia's existing target-date funds represents a 26-fold increase in fees with no documented justification. The absence of any comparative cost analysis directly contravenes PTE 2020-02's requirement for a prudent process. The undisclosed sales contest offering a $10,000 bonus and vacation trip is precisely the type of conflicted incentive that PTE 2020-02 prohibits, as the exemption bars financial institutions from using quotas, bonuses, or contests based on sales of specific products that could encourage advice contrary to the investor's best interest. Finally, the perfunctory checkbox documentation fails to demonstrate the care, skill, and diligence required. Granite Peak's own compliance memo acknowledged these obligations, making the firm's supervisory failure an additional aggravating factor. Neither Marcus nor Granite Peak can rely on PTE 2020-02 to excuse the prohibited transaction.
applicable_standard: ERISA §404(a)(1)(A)-(B) (duties of loyalty and prudence); ERISA §406(b) (prohibited transactions—self-dealing); PTE 2020-02 (Improving Investment Advice for Workers & Retirees), including best interest standard, conflict mitigation policies, and prohibition on sales contests; DOL Proposed Retirement Security Rule (October 31, 2023) expanding the definition of investment advice fiduciary under 29 CFR 2510.3-21
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: Marcus's undisclosed enrollment in a proprietary product sales contest directly violated PTE 2020-02's prohibition on compensation structures—such as quotas, bonuses, and contests—that incentivize recommendations contrary to the retirement investor's best interest.

fact_pattern:
Marcus Whitfield, age 58, is a longtime member of the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers (IBEW) Local 134 in Chicago. After 32 years of employment with Commonwealth Electric, Marcus is taking early retirement in March 2024. He has accumulated $487,000 in the IBEW-National Electrical Contractors Association (NECA) Pension Trust Fund, a collectively bargained defined benefit plan, and an additional $214,000 in the NECA-IBEW 401(k) Plan. Upon separation from employment, Marcus receives a packet from the plan administrator outlining his distribution options, including a lump-sum rollover.

Marcus visits Lakefront Wealth Advisors, a broker-dealer in downtown Chicago, where he meets with registered representative Dana Colbert. Dana is compensated primarily through commissions and receives an additional quarterly bonus when total assets under management in proprietary variable annuity products exceed $5 million. During the initial meeting on March 15, 2024, Dana reviews Marcus's pension and 401(k) statements and recommends that Marcus roll over both his DB lump sum ($487,000) and his 401(k) balance ($214,000) — a total of $701,000 — into a Lakefront-branded variable annuity product with a 7-year surrender schedule, a 1.45% annual mortality and expense charge, a 0.25% administrative fee, and underlying sub-account expenses averaging 0.85%. The total all-in annual cost would be approximately 2.55%. The variable annuity also pays Dana a 5.5% upfront commission ($38,555).

Dana does not discuss the option of Marcus leaving his assets in the collectively bargained plans, where the DB plan charges no direct fees to participants and the 401(k) plan offers a diversified lineup of institutional index funds with an average expense ratio of 0.06%. Dana does not document any analysis comparing the costs, investment options, or features of the existing plans versus the recommended variable annuity. Dana's written recommendation letter to Marcus states only that the variable annuity will provide 'tax-deferred growth and guaranteed income options for retirement,' without addressing the fee differential or the fact that IRA assets already enjoy tax-deferred treatment. Marcus signs the rollover paperwork on March 22, 2024.
question: Did Dana Colbert satisfy her fiduciary obligations under ERISA and applicable DOL standards when recommending that Marcus roll over $701,000 from his collectively bargained retirement plans into a high-cost proprietary variable annuity?
answer:
Dana Colbert violated her fiduciary obligations under ERISA and the DOL's fiduciary framework in multiple respects.

First, under the DOL's definition of fiduciary investment advice — which the 2016 Fiduciary Rule (81 Fed. Reg. 20945) and the 2024 Retirement Security Rule sought to clarify — a recommendation to roll over assets from an ERISA-covered plan constitutes fiduciary investment advice when it is individualized to the participant, provided for a fee, and made under circumstances indicating reliance. Dana's one-on-one recommendation to Marcus, for which she received a 5.5% commission, clearly meets all elements of the fiduciary definition. The rollover recommendation itself is the critical threshold: once Dana recommended that Marcus move assets out of the ERISA plans, she became a fiduciary with respect to that advice.

Second, ERISA §404(a)(1)(A) and (B) require a fiduciary to act solely in the interest of participants and beneficiaries and with the care, skill, prudence, and diligence that a prudent person would use. Dana's failure to conduct or document any comparative analysis of the existing plan options versus the variable annuity is a textbook prudence failure. The collectively bargained plans offered institutional pricing at 0.06% average expense — roughly 42 times less expensive than the 2.55% all-in cost of the variable annuity. A prudent fiduciary would have analyzed and documented this fee differential, the surrender charges, and the absence of any incremental tax benefit (since IRAs and qualified plans both offer tax deferral).

Third, the recommendation created a prohibited transaction under ERISA §406(b) because Dana's compensation was directly enhanced by the rollover — she received $38,555 in upfront commissions and contributed to her quarterly proprietary-product bonus. To rely on PTE 2020-02, Dana would need to satisfy its Impartial Conduct Standards, including the best interest standard, reasonable compensation requirement, and the obligation not to make materially misleading statements. Dana failed all three: the recommendation was not in Marcus's best interest given the massive fee disparity; the 2.55% annual cost plus 5.5% load is difficult to justify as reasonable for a near-retiree with low-cost plan alternatives; and her written recommendation omitted material facts about comparative costs and the redundancy of tax-deferral.

Dana has no viable defense. The fact that the variable annuity offers a guaranteed income rider does not cure the analysis gap — a prudent process requires weighing that feature against significantly higher costs and documenting why it serves the client's specific needs. No such documentation exists. This is a clear fiduciary breach.
applicable_standard: ERISA §404(a)(1)(A)-(B) (fiduciary duties of loyalty and prudence); ERISA §406(b) (prohibited transactions involving fiduciary self-dealing); DOL Definition of Fiduciary, 81 Fed. Reg. 20945 (2016); PTE 2020-02 Impartial Conduct Standards (best interest, reasonable compensation, no misleading statements); 29 CFR §2550.404a-1 (investment duties); DOL Retirement Security Rule (2024)
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: Dana failed to perform or document any comparative analysis of the low-cost collectively bargained plan options versus the high-cost proprietary variable annuity, while receiving a $38,555 commission that created an unmitigated conflict of interest.

fact_pattern:
Marcus Delgado is a registered representative of Pinnacle Financial Group, a dual-registered broker-dealer and RIA based in Charlotte, North Carolina. On March 15, 2017, Marcus met with Patricia Okonkwo, a 58-year-old public school teacher who had recently left her position after 26 years of service. Patricia had accumulated $387,000 in her employer-sponsored 403(b) plan administered by TIAA, which held a diversified mix of low-cost index funds with a weighted average expense ratio of 0.08%. Patricia contacted Marcus after seeing a mailer from Pinnacle offering 'free retirement planning consultations for educators.'

During the meeting, Marcus reviewed Patricia's 403(b) statement and recommended she roll the entire $387,000 balance into a new IRA at Pinnacle. He told Patricia that the IRA would give her 'more investment choices and better personalized service.' He did not discuss the option of leaving the assets in the 403(b) plan, nor did he compare the fees, investment options, or services available in the existing plan versus the proposed IRA. Marcus recommended allocating the IRA proceeds into a combination of Class A mutual funds carrying front-end loads averaging 4.75% and variable annuities with mortality and expense charges of 1.35% plus fund sub-account expenses averaging 0.85%. The total first-year cost to Patricia would include approximately $18,382 in front-end sales charges plus ongoing annual expenses exceeding $8,500—compared to approximately $310 annually in the 403(b) plan.

Marcus earned a $9,500 commission on the mutual fund sales and a $7,800 commission on the variable annuity placement. He did not execute any written acknowledgment of fiduciary status. Pinnacle had no written policies requiring its representatives to document the basis for rollover recommendations or to conduct comparative fee analyses between existing retirement plans and proposed IRAs. Marcus provided Patricia with standard brokerage account disclosures but did not provide any document specifically addressing conflicts of interest related to the rollover recommendation or the compensation differential between leaving assets in the 403(b) versus moving them to Pinnacle.
question: Under the DOL's 2016 Fiduciary Rule framework and applicable prohibited transaction provisions, did Marcus Delgado's rollover recommendation and subsequent investment of Patricia's retirement assets constitute a fiduciary act, and if so, did his conduct violate ERISA and Code fiduciary standards?
answer:
Marcus Delgado's conduct constitutes a clear violation of fiduciary standards under the DOL's 2016 Conflict of Interest Rule. The analysis proceeds on two levels: fiduciary status and prohibited transaction liability.

First, under the 2016 final rule amending 29 CFR §2510.3-21, Marcus qualifies as a fiduciary because he provided a recommendation to Patricia regarding the rollover of her 403(b) plan assets—an IRA rollover recommendation—for a fee or other compensation (commissions totaling $17,300). The 2016 rule was specifically designed to eliminate the narrow five-part test from the 1975 regulation, which had allowed advisers to avoid fiduciary status when providing one-time rollover recommendations. Under the revised definition, a person who makes a recommendation to roll over assets from an ERISA plan or 403(b) to an IRA, and who receives compensation in connection with that recommendation, is a fiduciary. Marcus's personalized recommendation to Patricia, directed at her specific retirement assets and made in the context of a compensated advisory relationship, satisfies this standard.

Second, as a fiduciary, Marcus is subject to ERISA §404(a)'s duty of prudence and loyalty and the prohibited transaction rules under ERISA §406 and Code §4975. His recommendation that Patricia move from a 0.08% expense ratio plan to investments costing over 2.2% annually—without any documented analysis of whether this served Patricia's interests—violates the duty of prudence under ERISA §404(a)(1)(B). Moreover, the commissions Marcus earned create a direct conflict of interest constituting a prohibited transaction under ERISA §406(b)(1) and Code §4975(c)(1)(E), as he used his fiduciary authority to generate compensation for himself.

To engage in these otherwise prohibited transactions, Marcus and Pinnacle would have needed to satisfy the conditions of the Best Interest Contract Exemption (BIC Exemption, PTE 2016-01), finalized concurrently with the 2016 rule. The BIC Exemption requires, among other things: (1) written acknowledgment of fiduciary status; (2) adherence to Impartial Conduct Standards including a best interest standard; (3) disclosure of material conflicts and compensation; and (4) institutional policies and procedures to mitigate conflicts. Marcus failed every one of these conditions—no fiduciary acknowledgment was executed, no comparative analysis was performed, no conflict disclosures were provided specific to the rollover, and Pinnacle maintained no policies requiring documentation of rollover rationale.

Pinnacle's institutional failure to maintain written supervisory procedures for rollover recommendations compounds the violation, as the BIC Exemption imposed firm-level compliance obligations. The absence of any defense under an applicable PTE renders both Marcus and Pinnacle liable for prohibited transactions, exposing them to excise taxes under Code §4975 and potential enforcement action by the DOL.
applicable_standard: 29 CFR §2510.3-21 (2016 Fiduciary Rule); ERISA §404(a)(1)(A)-(B) (duties of loyalty and prudence); ERISA §406(b)(1) (prohibited self-dealing transactions); IRC §4975(c)(1)(E) (prohibited transactions for IRAs); PTE 2016-01 (Best Interest Contract Exemption), including Impartial Conduct Standards and institutional compliance requirements
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: Marcus recommended a rollover generating $17,300 in personal commissions without performing or documenting any comparative analysis of fees, services, or investment options between the existing low-cost 403(b) plan and the proposed IRA, and without satisfying any exemption conditions to permit the conflicted transaction.

fact_pattern:
Pinnacle Retirement Services, LLC is a registered investment adviser and recordkeeper serving approximately 340 employer-sponsored 401(k) plans with combined assets of $8.2 billion. In March 2024, Pinnacle launches a financial wellness program called "RetireReady" for participants of its largest client, Greystone Manufacturing Corp.'s 401(k) plan, which has 4,200 participants and $620 million in plan assets. The RetireReady program consists of automated emails, webinars, and an interactive online portal that provides participants with general information about asset allocation principles, the power of compound interest, the importance of diversification, the effect of fees on long-term investment returns, and the general tax consequences of taking early distributions versus rolling assets into an IRA at separation from service.

Maria Calderon, age 58, is a Greystone participant with a $412,000 account balance who is considering early retirement. She logs into the RetireReady portal and receives a series of educational screens that explain, in general terms, that participants nearing retirement should consider their time horizon, risk tolerance, and income needs. The portal includes generic asset allocation models (e.g., 'conservative,' 'moderate,' 'aggressive') keyed to general age ranges but does not reference any specific investment options in the Greystone plan, nor does it suggest that Maria select any particular fund, model portfolio, or take any specific distribution action. Each screen carries a prominent disclaimer stating: 'This information is educational only and does not constitute a recommendation to buy or sell any investment or to take any distribution. Please consult a qualified financial adviser for personalized advice.'

Separately, when Maria calls Pinnacle's participant services line to ask about rolling her balance into an IRA, the call center representative, Jake Thornton, follows a scripted protocol. Jake explains the general differences between keeping assets in the plan versus rolling over to an IRA, including fee structures, investment option breadth, creditor protections under ERISA versus state law, and required minimum distribution rules. Jake does not recommend that Maria roll over, stay in the plan, or choose any specific IRA provider. He provides Maria with a checklist of factors to consider and suggests she may want to speak with a financial adviser for a personalized recommendation. The call is recorded and reviewed by Pinnacle's compliance department within 48 hours as part of its standard quality assurance process.
question: Under the DOL's proposed Retirement Security Rule redefining 'investment advice fiduciary,' does Pinnacle's RetireReady educational program and Jake Thornton's call center interaction with Maria Calderon constitute fiduciary investment advice triggering ERISA fiduciary obligations?
answer:
